question.text:
You are a portfolio manager provided with the expected return and standard deviation of four assets. Asset A: Expected Mean Return: 5%, Standard Deviation: 0; Asset B: Expected Mean Return: 10%, Standard Deviation: 10%; Asset C: Expected Mean Return: 12%, Standard Deviation: 15%; Asset D: Expected Mean Return: 7%, Standard Deviation: 17%.
Which asset would a conservative investor likely avoid?

explanation.text: The Logic: A conservative investor minimises downside by preferring lower standard deviation. Asset D has the highest SD at 17% yet delivers only 7% expected return — a poor risk-return trade-off that a conservative investor would actively avoid. The Trap: C tempts because 15% SD is visually close to D's 17%, but C at least compensates with 12% return. The trap is scoring assets only on risk or only on return in isolation; a conservative investor looks at the return-for-risk ratio, and D is the worst offender. Cross-Exam Context: Dominated-asset logic and conservative-investor suitability feature in NISM-Series-X-A, X-B, XXI-B and XVII (Retirement Adviser). Distributor's Pro-Tip: When a conservative client asks about a high-SD / low-return product (hybrid debt-equity funds often sit here), show them a dominated-asset chart — it kills the pitch faster than any verbal explanation.
